Screen a pile of filings for the ones worth reading

Source: R/xbrl_screen.R
xbrl_screen.Rd

Runs the package's checks over every filing in x and returns what they found, one row per finding, ranked so that the filings worth a closer look come first. It is the question to ask of a corpus before trusting it, or of a company before reading its report: where does this not add up, and how much does it matter?

Usage

xbrl_screen(
  x,
  basis = c("parent", "consolidated"),
  what = c("auditor", "balance", "income", "cashflow", "continuity"),
  materiality = 0.01,
  standardise = TRUE
)

Arguments

x

A tibble from read_xbrl(): any number of filings, any number of companies. Several years of the same company add the checks between filings. From xbrl_validate(), the checks it ran are read rather than run again.

basis

"parent" and "consolidated", the default, screens both; a group's cash flow statement is usually only consolidated.

what

Which checks to run: any of "auditor", "balance", "income", "cashflow" and "continuity". All of them by default.

materiality

Share of total assets under which a finding moves down a level. Default 0.01.

standardise

Put the tagging right before screening, with xbrl_standardise(): figures in the wrong unit, and cash flow signs an activity adds up only reversed. Default TRUE. See the section below.

Value

A tibble with one row per finding, most severe and largest first: the key (cvr, name, period_start, period_end), basis, check, finding, amount (the gap in the reporting currency, where the check gives one), share (amount against total assets), severity, detail (what the check said, in its own words), the filing's background – class, form, assurance, in_group, group_accounts, from xbrl_company() – and file. Filings with no finding have no rows; attr(s, "screened") says how many were looked at. It prints as one line per filing, its most serious finding first; the rows underneath are an ordinary tibble.

What it looks for

Each finding comes from a check that can be run on its own, and check names it:

  • "auditor" – the auditor qualified the opinion, gave an adverse one or none at all, or drew attention to a material uncertainty about the company continuing as a going concern (xbrl_company()). The first three are an auditor saying the accounts are wrong or cannot be judged, and rank with the arithmetic; the last is a risk, not an error.

  • "balance sheet" – the debit side does not equal the credit side, or one line is stated twice with two amounts (check_statement()).

  • "income statement" – a step of the cascade that no assignment of signs explains (check_cascade()).

  • "cash flow" – the statement does not add up, does not roll the cash forward, or closes on a cash figure the balance sheet does not carry; or it reports borrowing the balance sheet does not owe, the pattern of a grant booked as a loan (check_cashflow()).

  • "between filings" – a balance that reopened on a different amount in the next filing (check_continuity()). Income statement comparatives are left out, because they are reclassified routinely. With standardise = FALSE, also a figure written in the other unit.

The tagging first, the accounts second

A figure tagged in thousands where the filing is in kroner is a fact about the tagging, not about the company. Screened as it stands it outranks every real finding: in a 4,304-filing corpus, 41 of the 54 serious findings were that, and once the figures are standardised the 13 left are all cash flow statements that do not add up. So by default the figures are standardised first, and the screen looks at the accounts as they were meant. What was corrected, and what could not be settled, is kept apart in attr(s, "technical") and named in one line when the screen prints. standardise = FALSE screens the figures as tagged, and then a figure in the other unit is a finding of its own.

How it ranks

By how much a finding would change what a reader takes from the accounts. share is the amount against the filing's total assets, and severity combines the kind of finding with its size:

  • "high" – an auditor's qualified, adverse or missing opinion, or the statements do not hold together: a balance sheet whose sides differ, a cash flow statement that does not add up, or borrowing the balance sheet does not owe with its other half found elsewhere in the statement. Unstandardised, also a figure off by a factor of a thousand.

  • "medium" – a going concern uncertainty, or something is unexplained but the statements still close: borrowing without debt to match, an income statement step no signs explain, a line stated with two amounts.

  • "low" – a lead: a figure restated between filings.

A finding under materiality of total assets moves down one level, so a rounding difference on a large company does not sit above a real one on a small company, and one that ends at "low" that way is left out. A finding with no amount keeps its level.

What it does not do

A finding is a reason to read the report, not a conclusion about it. Every one has an innocent explanation as well as a guilty one, and the checks cannot tell them apart: a restatement can be a correction of policy or of an error, borrowing without debt can be a facility drawn and repaid within the year. The function says where to look.

It does not look at the prose or at anything the filing did not tag. A misstatement that is consistent everywhere, scaled or restated throughout, is invisible inside one filing and is found only between filings, so pass several years to see that kind.

See also

xbrl_accounts(), whose checks table answers the same questions as yes or no; check_statement(), check_cascade(), check_cashflow() and check_continuity() for the detail behind a finding.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")
s <- xbrl_screen(x)
s

# the filings with something serious, one row each
s[s$severity == "high" & !duplicated(s$file), ]
} # }
